newsitem.title: USA: Mutual fund demand from 401k plans seen cresting.
newsitem.headline: Mutual fund demand from 401k plans seen cresting.

text.p: The demand for mutual funds from retirement accounts, specifically 401(k) plans, will crest within a few years after a period of rapid growth, according to a study released on Monday.

Increasing demand for alternative investment vehicles, such as separately managed and commingled accounts, will cause a massive shift to mutual funds in recent years to level off around the turn of the century, the study said.

Separately managed and commingled accounts differ from mutual funds in that they allow the retirement plan sponsors to exert more control over investments decisions, said Glen Casey, an author of the study, which was conducted by Cerulli Associates Inc and Lipper Analytical Services Inc.
Plan sponsors are tired of the "chasing of performance, the lack of adherence to style and objectives" with many mutual funds, he said.
Many are wary of the so-called Magellan effect, he said, referring to Fidelity Investments' Magellan Fund, which strayed from its perceived style last year by making massive investments into bonds.
Firms positioned to capitalize on the shift include Morgan Stanley Group, J.P. Morgan & Co Inc and State Street Boston Corp, said Cerulli's Casey.
By 1996, the percentage of 401(k) assets in mutual funds rose to an estimated 38 percent from nine percent in 1986, according to the study.
But the trend will level off by the end of the decade, and mutual funds should account for about 45 percent of the $1.5 trillion 401(k) market by 2001, the study found.
Meanwhile, the market share of the dominant mutual fund companies in the battle for 401(k) assets will stagnate or decline as the business becomes more institutionalized, the study said.

The institutionalization of the 401(k) market will diminsh the importance of the retail strengths of the major mutual fund companies, such as brand-name recognition, daily price valuations and investor communications.
The change will pave the way for investment firms already in institutional markets, such as defined benefit plans, foundations and endowments.
The push to cut investment costs is one of the drivers behind the institutionalization of the market, and plan sponsors will bear more of the associated costs themselves, the study said.

"We believe that plan sponsors are becoming increasingly wary of their participants paying a significant premium for name-brand recognition, daily valuations and transactions, and other inherent advantages associated with retail mutual funds," the study said.
Cerulli Associates is a Boston-based consulting firm, and Lipper, based in New York, provides research on investment companies.
